messages.subject: stan and compositional data
parts:
Good morning,
could you please help me to find an example in STAN for handling data that has a normal distribution on the simplex?
I would start with something simple like estimating the means of the components (the sum of the three means is constrained to be 1).

I just need something to start working on, so any help is appreciated.

I have found a toy dataset in the "compositional" package in CRAN.

library(compositions)
GeoChemSed=read.csv("http://www.stat.boogaart.de/compositionsRBook/geochemsed.csv",header=TRUE, skip=1)
x=compositions::acomp(GeoChemSed, parts=c("Cr","Zn","Pb"))

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: stan and compositional data
parts:
Dr. Carpenter,
I'm new to composition, so I am just sticking to my gun, i.e. Van Den Boogart & Tolosana-Delgado, "Analyzing Compositional Data with R" from the UseR! collection. Some aspect of compositions are still obscure for me.

A D-part simplex is defined as:
S^D := \left \{\mathbf{x}=(x_1, ...,x_D): x_i \geq 0, \sum_{i=1}^{D} x_i=1\right \}

( see book 2.5.1 pag 37)

so the simplex of D=3 represent a ternary diagram, where the three components are projected in baricentric coordinates, and if D=4 we are working on on a regular tetrahedron. The toy dataset I found yesterday (D=3) is plotted in the file attached.
A random composition X has a normal distribution on the simplex (or additive logistic normal) with mean vector m and variance matrix Sigma,, if projecting it onto any arbitrary direction of the simplex u, with the Aitchison scalar product  yelds a random variable with a univariate normal distribution.... and the joint density [...] is:
f(x; \mu_v, \Sigma_v) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^{(D-1)}\cdot \left | |Sigma_v \right |}} exp\left [ -\frac{1}{2}(ilr(x)-\mu_v)\cdot \Sigma_v^{-1} \cdot (ilr(x)-\mu_v)^t\right ]

The Aitchison scalar product is defined as:
\left \langle x,y \right \rangle_A=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i>j}^{D}ln\frac{x_i}{x_j}ln\frac{y_i}{y_j}

and the ilr() is the (I cite the book at page 42) the "so-called isometric log-ratio transformation".
Ok. I think I am a little overshooting my competences. For this reason I am asking help.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: stan and compositional data
parts:
> On Jul 5, 2016, at 1:37 AM, Fabio Zottele <fabio....@fmach.it> wrote:
>
> Dr. Carpenter,
> I'm new to composition, so I am just sticking to my gun, i.e. Van Den Boogart & Tolosana-Delgado, "Analyzing Compositional Data with R" from the UseR! collection. Some aspect of compositions are still obscure for me.
>
> A D-part simplex is defined as:
> S^D := \left \{\mathbf{x}=(x_1, ...,x_D): x_i \geq 0, \sum_{i=1}^{D} x_i=1\right \}
>
> ( see book 2.5.1 pag 37)

That's the usual notion of simplex and it's what the simplex type
in Stan guarantees.
> so the simplex of D=3 represent a ternary diagram, where the three components are projected in baricentric coordinates,

I don't know what baricentric is, but you can definitely plot
a 3-simplex as a triangle plot.
> and if D=4 we are working on on a regular tetrahedron.
You can think of the bounds of the simplex being where one component is 1.

> The toy dataset I found yesterday (D=3) is plotted in the file attached.
> A random composition X has a normal distribution on the simplex (or additive logistic normal)

I thought you might've meant logistic normal. That's easy

parameters {
vector[K] theta_raw;

transformed parameters {
simplex[K] theta;
theta = softmax(theta_raw);

model {
theta_raw ~ multi_normal(m, Sigma);

This transforms the multivariate normal theta_raw onto the simplex.
It has one too many degrees of freedom this way, you can
parameterize it using a (K-1)-dimensional multi-normal and pin one
dimension to 0 for identifiability.

parameters {
vector[K-1] theta_raw;

transformed parameters {
simplex[K] theta;
theta[1] = 0;
theta[2:K] = theta_raw;
theta = softmax(theta);

model {
theta_raw ~ multi_normal(m, Sigma); // now m and Sigma sizes K-1 and (K-1)x(K-1)

> with mean vector m and variance matrix Sigma,, if projecting it onto any arbitrary direction of the simplex u, with the Aitchison scalar product yelds a random variable with a univariate normal distribution.... and the joint density [...] is:
> f(x; \mu_v, \Sigma_v) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^{(D-1)}\cdot \left | |Sigma_v \right |}} exp\left [ -\frac{1}{2}(ilr(x)-\mu_v)\cdot \Sigma_v^{-1} \cdot (ilr(x)-\mu_v)^t\right ]
>
> The Aitchison scalar product is defined as:
> \left \langle x,y \right \rangle_A=\frac{1}{D}\sum_{i>j}^{D}ln\frac{x_i}{x_j}ln\frac{y_i}{y_j}

No idea what any of this is, I'm afraid, but you won't need it for
the logistic multi-normal.
> and the ilr() is the (I cite the book at page 42) the "so-called isometric log-ratio transformation".

That's probably just a fancy name for what the rest of us
call softmax

softmax(v) = exp(v) / sum(exp(v))

It projects a vector in R^N onto the N-simplex.
> Ok. I think I am a little overshooting my competences. For this reason I am asking help.

I'd suggest starting simple and working up to the
distributions you really want.

You still haven't said what you wanted to do with it and if
m and Sigma are parameters or data. If they're parameters,
you want to use the Cholesky parameterization as described
in the regression chapter of the manual.

- Bob

Hi all, and thanks for the help so far.
I searched the manual and forums and at the end I got a clearer idea about STAN and simplexes.
Now I've got
1) one STAN script to generate a sample of random point  (y) extracted from a multivariate normal distribution (with given Mean and Sigma ) projected on a simplex. To make it simple i limited to a 3D simplex.
2) one STAN script to estimate M (sample mean) and S (sample variance-covariance matrix) from the data produced by script1
3)one R script to rule'em all.

I will focus now on STAN script 1, because the output values are not my expected ones.
In R I defne the true mean (it must be a simplex) and the true Sigma.

Mean.true = data.frame(A= 0.1, B= 0.3, C= 0.6) 
Sigma.true = matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.5), byrow= TRUE, nrow= 3)
generatorData = list(Sigma= Sigma.true, mu= as.numeric(Mean.true))
model= stan(file= "simplexGenerator.stan", data= generatorData, iter= 100, chains= 1, warmup= 0, algorithm= "Fixed_param", verbose= FALSE)

}

    vector[2] mu2;

}

}

}

generated quantities {
    vector[2] theta_raw;
    simplex[3] theta;
   
    theta_raw =  multi_normal_rng(mu2, Sigma2);
   
    theta[1] = 0;
    theta[2:3] = theta_raw;
    theta = softmax(theta);
   
}

I retrieve the values:

values= rstan::extract(model, inc_warmup=FALSE, permuted=TRUE)
colnames(y) = c("A","B","C")
Mean.sample= data.frame(A= mean(y[,1]), B= mean(y[,2]), C= mean(y[,3]))

Now, y is a simplex(OK!) and Mean.sample is a simplex too (Yeah!) but if I plot the Y on a ternary diagram with the true mean (dark red) and the sample mean (dark green) I see that these two last simplexes are far away (I attach the ternary.jpeg image as reference).
Have I missed something? (a reprojection maybe...).
The deviates are even more clearer if i plot the densities of the sample on the three axes (I attach density.jpeg as reference, the True mean is in dark red, the sample mean is in dark green).

Moreover, being a STAN newbie: is the stan file correct or there is room for improvement in the various sections?

As ever, any help is appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] stan and compositional data
parts:
You need to put those means on the logit scale.

> aaa = c(.1, .3, .6)

And then look at softmax:

> exp(aaa) / sum(exp(aaa))
[1] 0.2583897 0.3155978 0.4260125

You can't just grab two components. You have to solve for
the other two given that one of them's going to be fixed.

And it's also overparameterized (leading to non-identification)
with three values. There are only two degrees of freedom
in a 3-simplex (because theta[3] = 1 - theta[1] - theta[2]).

- Bob
